## Chapter 4: Reducing Attention Cost: Windows, Sparsity, `#linebreak()`{=typst}and Latent KV Representations {#sec-ch4}

*Three Different Problems, Not One Knob*

### Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- Explain why full causal attention grows expensive as retained
  context grows, without conflating score-matrix cost, KV-cache
  storage, total model FLOPs, wall-clock latency, memory bandwidth,
  and temporary workspace.
- Distinguish *attending to fewer positions* from *storing a smaller
  representation per position* as independent axes, and explain why
  sparse attention does not automatically shrink the KV-cache.
- Draw sliding-window attention's receptive field across stacked
  layers, and state the conceptual purpose of occasional global layers
  or tokens.
- Compare GQA and MLA structurally (GQA shares $K$/$V$ heads; MLA
  compresses what is stored per token) and state what a DeepSeek-style
  MLA cache retains, including why a separately-retained rotary
  component is needed.
- Explain why an optimized MLA implementation need not reconstruct
  full $K$/$V$ tensors every decode step, and recognize recurrent/
  linear-state alternatives as a third design family without claiming
  this chapter teaches their mechanics.

### Why this matters

Chapter 3 fixed *how many* query heads share a key/value head. This
chapter is about a different question entirely: given a fixed head
structure, what else can shrink attention's cost as retained context
grows? Three genuinely different strategies exist -- attend to fewer
positions, store less per retained position, or replace the growing
history with something that doesn't grow -- and they solve different
problems. Treating them as interchangeable, or as three strengths of
one dial, is the single biggest misreading this chapter is built to
prevent.

### Mental model or analogy

Think of the retained context as a shelf of books a reader might need
again. Strategy 1 (fewer positions) means only checking nearby shelves.
Strategy 2 (smaller representation) means keeping one compressed
summary card per book instead of the whole book. Strategy 3 (replace
growing state) means keeping a running summary that never grows,
discarding the shelf entirely. A reader who confuses "check fewer
shelves" with "keep shorter notes" would misjudge what they can still
find later -- exactly the confusion this chapter targets.

### Visual overview

![Three different axes for reducing attention's cost, not one
continuum: which positions are scored, what is stored per retained
position, and whether the history grows at all. Panel 3 names the
third family without teaching its
mechanics.](figures/rendered/fig-three-efficiency-strategies.svg){#fig-three-strategies}

### Technical core

**Full attention's baseline.** For a sequence of retained length $S$,
the attention score matrix has $S^2$ entries per head -- full attention
costs $O(S^2)$ score computations for a whole sequence. During
incremental decoding, each single new query attends over all $S$
retained positions, so per-step attention work grows with $S$; summed
over $S$ decode steps this totals $O(S^2)$ as well. The **KV-cache**,
by contrast, grows *linearly* in $S$ (per @eq-kv-cache from Chapter 3)
-- storage and score-computation are different growth curves, and
neither is the same as total model FLOPs (which includes the
feed-forward sublayers), wall-clock latency (hardware- and
batch-dependent), memory bandwidth (the rate data moves, not the
amount), or temporary softmax/attention workspace (excluded from the
cache formula entirely).

**Sliding-window attention.** Each position attends only to a bounded
window of $W$ recent positions -- the *direct* receptive field is $W$,
regardless of $S$. Stacking layers extends this indirectly:

$$
\text{effective receptive field after } L \text{ stacked windowed layers} = L \times W
$$ {#eq-receptive-field}

For $W=4$ over 3 stacked layers, the direct window per layer stays 4,
but the effective reach grows to $3 \times 4 = 12$ (verified
programmatically) -- wider than one layer's window, but still not
unrestricted global attention.

![A target position's direct window is narrow at any one layer;
tracing back through earlier layers, the region of positions that can
indirectly influence it widens by $W$ per layer -- distinct from
unrestricted global
attention.](figures/rendered/fig-sliding-window-receptive-field.svg){#fig-sliding-window-rf}

@fig-sliding-window-rf marks direct vs.
indirect reach explicitly. If a layer strictly evicts state outside its
window, that layer's cache growth can be bounded; real serving systems
may still retain more state than the strictest bound, depending on
implementation. Real models often mix strategies: most layers windowed,
a minority full ("global") layers, or selected global tokens visible to
every position -- recovering long-range access without paying full
attention's cost everywhere. Mistral 7B's window-4096 design with a
rolling-buffer cache is one deployed example, reporting roughly an 8x
cache reduction at 32K context versus full attention ([@src-25]).

**Sparse attention.** A sparse pattern (e.g. strided/block
factorizations, [@src-26]) restricts *which* query-key pairs are
scored, reducing $O(S^2)$ score computation. This is a different
statement from what must stay *cached*: some patterns permit dropping
positions no future query will ever revisit, but others (e.g. a
strided pattern where a future layer or a future token's stride
offset can reach any past position) must retain every token's $K$/$V$
regardless, because some future query may still access it.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"Sparse attention automatically means a proportionally smaller KV
cache."** It does not. Sparsity is a statement about which pairs get
*scored*; the cache must hold whatever a *future* query might still
need, which depends on the specific pattern, not sparsity alone.
:::

**Multi-head latent attention (MLA).** GQA (Chapter 3) shares whole
$K$/$V$ *heads* across query groups -- the per-head representation is
unchanged, just fewer distinct copies. MLA changes *what* is stored
per token: DeepSeek-V2 ([@src-27]) jointly compresses $K$ and $V$ into
one shared latent $c_t^{KV} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_c}$ per token per layer,
with $d_c \ll H_q\, d_{\text{head}}$, via a down-projection; per-head
$K$/$V$ are then *derived* from that latent when needed, not stored
directly. RoPE complicates this: rotating the compressed latent
directly would tie the up-projection to a position-specific rotation
matrix that cannot later be folded elsewhere, forcing every prior
token's key to be recomputed at each step. MLA's fix retains a small,
separately-cached decoupled rotary component ($d_{\text{rope}}$,
shared across heads) alongside the latent, so:

$$
M_{\text{MLA}} = B \, S \, L \, (d_c + d_{\text{rope}}) \, \text{bytes\_per\_elem}
$$ {#eq-mla-cache}

@eq-mla-cache and Chapter 3's $M_{KV}$ describe **different cached
representations** -- a numeric comparison is meaningful only for an
explicitly defined architecture, and both remain logical minimums
(runtime overhead excluded, same exclusions as Chapter 3).

::: {.callout-warning title="Common misconception"}
**"MLA is just GQA with fewer KV heads."** It is not. GQA shares whole
per-head $K$/$V$ representations across query groups; MLA compresses
$K$ and $V$ *jointly* into one smaller latent representation per
token, a different mechanism, not a further point on GQA's
head-count axis.
:::

![MLA's cache pathway: only the compressed latent and the decoupled
rotary component are cached. Reconstructing full K/V (left) is always
a conceptually valid derivation; an optimized implementation may
instead take the dashed, optional matrix-absorption path, which never
materializes full K/V at
all.](figures/rendered/fig-mla-cache-pathway.svg){#fig-mla-pathway}

@fig-mla-pathway shows what is actually cached and where reconstruction
happens. Because a score is $q_t^\top k_j = q_t^\top (W^{UK} c_j^{KV})$,
and matrix multiplication reassociates as $(q_t^\top W^{UK})
c_j^{KV}$, an optimized implementation can fold $W^{UK}$ into the
query-side projection ahead of time (and, symmetrically, $W^{UV}$ into
the output projection) -- so it never has to materialize full $K$/$V$
at all ([@src-27]). This is an available optimization, not a mandatory
step every implementation takes; the conceptual derivation (reconstruct,
then attend) remains valid either way.

### Worked example

**Sliding-window reach.** $W=4$, layers 1/2/3 give effective reach
4/8/12 (@eq-receptive-field, verified programmatically).

**GQA vs. MLA cache.** Reusing Chapter 3's base config ($L=32$,
$H_q=32$, $d_{\text{head}}=128$, $S=8192$, $B=1$, bf16) and DeepSeek-V2's
own reported ratio ($d_c = 4\,d_{\text{head}} = 512$,
$d_{\text{rope}} = 0.5\,d_{\text{head}} = 64$; [@src-27] Table 1):

| Representation | Per-sequence cache | vs. MHA (4 GiB) |
|---|---|---|
| GQA, $H_{kv}=8$ (Ch. 3) | 1 GiB | 0.25x |
| MLA, $d_c{+}d_{\text{rope}}=576$ | 288 MiB | 0.070x |

: GQA vs. MLA on one shared base config -- verified programmatically; see the Build and Version Note {#tbl-gqa-mla-worked}

This MLA configuration's cache equals a GQA config with exactly 2.25
groups ([@src-27]'s own stated equivalence, reproduced here as a
verified invariant) -- MLA and GQA can land at comparable *sizes* for
some configuration, without being the same mechanism. This toy ratio
is **not** a claimed speedup: cache compression is not the same as
end-to-end latency, model quality and training behavior are outside
this arithmetic, and runtime overhead is excluded throughout.

### Compare and contrast

| | Full attn. | Sliding-window | Sparse (generic) | GQA | MLA | Recurrent/linear |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Changes connectivity? | -- | yes | yes | no | no | yes (different primitive) |
| Changes stored representation? | -- | pattern-dependent | pattern-dependent | yes (fewer copies) | yes (compressed) | yes (fixed-size state) |
| Can bound retained history? | no | pattern-dependent | pattern-dependent | no | no | yes |
| Direct access to every prior token? | yes | no (indirect only) | pattern-dependent | yes | yes (via latent) | no |
| Primary benefit | -- | compute + memory | compute | memory/bandwidth | memory/bandwidth | memory + compute |
| Principal tradeoff | cost grows with $S$ | indirect long-range access | cache not guaranteed smaller | some capacity loss | implementation complexity | mechanics not covered here |

: Six strategies compared without forcing false binaries -- "pattern-dependent" and "implementation-dependent" are answers, not omissions {#tbl-strategy-comparison}

### Applied exercise

A workload needs long context, high concurrency, and occasional
retrieval of very old tokens. Explain why a pure sliding window may be
insufficient, and what combination of mechanisms (global layers/
tokens, GQA, MLA) could help.

### Interview lens

*"Compare GQA, sliding-window attention, and MLA. What resource does
each primarily reduce, and what does each give up or complicate?"* A
strong answer names each one's primary win and cost: GQA (memory/
bandwidth, at some representational cost), sliding-window (compute
and memory, at the cost of indirect long-range access), and MLA
(memory/bandwidth, at the cost of implementation complexity) -- and
does not collapse any two into the same mechanism.

### Chapter recap

- Full attention's score matrix grows $O(S^2)$; its KV-cache grows
  linearly in $S$ -- different curves, never the same claim.
- Attending to fewer positions (windows, sparsity) and storing less
  per position (MLA) are independent axes; sparse attention does not
  automatically shrink the cache.
- Sliding-window's reach is $W$; stacked layers reach $L \times W$
  indirectly -- not unrestricted global attention.
- MLA compresses $K$/$V$ jointly into one latent per token (plus a
  rotary component); GQA shares whole per-head copies instead --
  different mechanisms, occasionally comparable sizes.
- An optimized MLA implementation may skip explicit $K$/$V$
  reconstruction via matrix absorption, but this is an available
  optimization, not a mandatory step.
- Recurrent/SSM/linear-attention replace the growing cache with a
  fixed-size state -- named here as a third family, mechanics deferred.
